item.title: Thanksgiving night sky 2026 — What to look for after dinner tonight
item.description: null If your household is like most American families, then on Thursday you likely will all be sitting down with family and friends for a traditional Thanksgiving turkey dinner during the mid-to-late afternoon hours. Then as darkness falls, some will probably migrate into the living room to catch some football or other holiday fare on television. But if you have a large gathering of family and friends at your home — and if your skies are mainly clear — why not invite everyone outside to gaze at the evening sky? If you have binoculars, or better yet, a telescope, you just might end up turning this into a memorable family tradition of its own. First, the "Lord of the Rings" . . . If I may paraphrase the mysterious voice from the 1989 movie, "Field of Dreams": "If you set up your telescope, they will come." And you'll get a big kick out of your Turkey Day guests uttering all the "oohs" and "ahs" or exclamations of "Wow!" with just one peek through the eyepiece. As darkness falls, Saturn will glow at first magnitude, shining with a sedate, yellow-white light and appearing noticeably brighter than the star Fomalhaut, about 40 degrees (the equivalent of four fist-widths) to its lower right. Its famous ring system is now tilted only about six degrees toward Earth but may be visible with steadied (or image-stabilized) high-power binoculars or through the eyepiece of a telescope magnifying over 30-power. The rings will seem to glow with an inner light and for those who have never had the pleasure of seeing them for themselves, that first view always elicits astonishment; kids especially most often will say: "Awesome!" or "No way!" I've even had people accuse me of using a slide of Saturn, to which I, of course, reply with, "No . . . that's the real thing." Saturn will shine high in the southern sky on Nov. 26. (Image credit: Starry Night Pro 8) . . . and later, the moon Then, along about 6:25 p.m. local time, the waning gibbous moon, 2½ days past full phase and 91% illuminated, will begin to emerge from beyond the east-northeast horizon. Give it another hour and it will stand about 10 degrees above the horizon — equal to the width of your clenched fist held at arm's length. By then, the moon will be in a better position for evening study. Location of the moon at approximately 9p.m. on Thanksgiving. Local moonrise and moonset times will vary depending on your location. (Image credit: Starry Night Pro 8 ) Even in binoculars, the moon is a striking sight to see. It's such a special object because it doesn't matter whether you live in a rural area or in the middle of a brightly lit city, for the moon can always be readily observed. It always looks spectacular whether you're using binoculars or a telescope. It never looks precisely the same no matter how often you view it and can be observed even on hazy or partially cloud-covered nights. item.dc:creator: Joe Rao
item.content:encoded: null If your household is like most American families, then on Thursday you likely will all be sitting down with family and friends for a traditional Thanksgiving turkey dinner during the mid-to-late afternoon hours. Then as darkness falls, some will probably migrate into the living room to catch some football or other holiday fare on television. But if you have a large gathering of family and friends at your home — and if your skies are mainly clear — why not invite everyone outside to gaze at the evening sky? If you have binoculars, or better yet, a telescope, you just might end up turning this into a memorable family tradition of its own. First, the "Lord of the Rings" . . . If I may paraphrase the mysterious voice from the 1989 movie, "Field of Dreams": "If you set up your telescope, they will come." And you'll get a big kick out of your Turkey Day guests uttering all the "oohs" and "ahs" or exclamations of "Wow!" with just one peek through the eyepiece. As darkness falls, Saturn will glow at first magnitude, shining with a sedate, yellow-white light and appearing noticeably brighter than the star Fomalhaut, about 40 degrees (the equivalent of four fist-widths) to its lower right. Its famous ring system is now tilted only about six degrees toward Earth but may be visible with steadied (or image-stabilized) high-power binoculars or through the eyepiece of a telescope magnifying over 30-power. The rings will seem to glow with an inner light and for those who have never had the pleasure of seeing them for themselves, that first view always elicits astonishment; kids especially most often will say: "Awesome!" or "No way!" I've even had people accuse me of using a slide of Saturn, to which I, of course, reply with, "No . . . that's the real thing." Saturn will shine high in the southern sky on Nov. 26. (Image credit: Starry Night Pro 8) . . . and later, the moon Then, along about 6:25 p.m. local time, the waning gibbous moon, 2½ days past full phase and 91% illuminated, will begin to emerge from beyond the east-northeast horizon. Give it another hour and it will stand about 10 degrees above the horizon — equal to the width of your clenched fist held at arm's length. By then, the moon will be in a better position for evening study. Location of the moon at approximately 9p.m. on Thanksgiving. Local moonrise and moonset times will vary depending on your location. (Image credit: Starry Night Pro 8 ) Even in binoculars, the moon is a striking sight to see. It's such a special object because it doesn't matter whether you live in a rural area or in the middle of a brightly lit city, for the moon can always be readily observed. It always looks spectacular whether you're using binoculars or a telescope. It never looks precisely the same no matter how often you view it and can be observed even on hazy or partially cloud-covered nights. Pay particular attention to the line of darkness — called the terminator — features near that border stand out in bold relief; the shadows become stronger and details are more easily seen. Take note on this night of the circular dark area, bisected by the terminator: Mare Crisium — the "Sea of Crises." Immediately bordering above it is a 50-mile (80 km)-wide ring of very rugged mountains, rising as high as 14,400 feet (4,389 meters), which now resembles a huge crater partially in shadow when the sun is low. A bonus: A view of the International Space Station Probably the one object that your Thanksgiving guests will want to see is the biggest and brightest of all the man-made objects orbiting the Earth: the International Space Station (ISS). Except for those living across the southern US, for most everywhere else, the ISS will be making visible passes on Thanksgiving evening. International Space Station pass over Morteratsch, Graubunden, Switzerland. (Image credit: Roberto Moiola / Sysaworld via Getty Images) Circling the Earth at an average altitude of 260 miles (420 km) and at a speed of 17,500 mph (28,200 kph), it can appear to move as fast as a high-flying jet airliner, sometimes taking as much as six or seven minutes to cross the sky. It can easily be confused with aircraft lights. Nominally, it appears white with a slight yellow tinge and at its very brightest it can sometimes appear to shine as bright as magnitude -5.6, which is twice as bright as the planet Venus! So, what is the viewing schedule on Thanksgiving for your hometown? You can easily find out by visiting one of three popular websites: Spot the Station This site will tell you when and where to sight the ISS. All you need do is type in your city or town, then click on the map pinpoint to get all the details. You can even sign up to get email or text alerts when the space station is flying over. Chris Peat's Heavens Above This site will not only provide you with sighting information for the ISS, but also for many other satellites as well. You must first register and then you can input your location to generate a sighting schedule. Live Real-Time Satellite Tracking Like Heavens Above, you can get sighting information for the ISS and other satellites. Once you log on this site will automatically provide details based on your IP address ... or you can set a "custom" location. Here at Space.com, we like to wish a very happy and safe Thanksgiving to all, and of course, clear skies! Joe Rao serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium . He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine , Sky and Telescope , The Old Farmer's Almanac and other publications.

item.title: Remembering Pete Edochie: 5 Films That Made Him a Nollywood Legend
item.description: Nollywood icon Pete Edochie, MON, who passed away at the age of 79 in Enugu. Did you grow up watching Pete Edochie in Nollywood films? Then you probably remember that voice. Deep, commanding and unmistakable, it often came with his signature red cap, traditional Igbo attire and a generous helping of proverbs. The actor was just as memorable away from the screen, where his sharp wit, outspoken nature and candid opinions made him a fascinating personality in interviews. He was never one to shy away from saying exactly what he thought, and that straightforwardness became another part of what audiences remembered about him. For generations of Nollywood viewers, Pete Edochie was the actor they could recognise before he had even finished his first sentence. He became one of Nigerian cinema’s most familiar faces, often playing kings, chiefs, fathers and respected elders. His breakthrough came in 1987 when he portrayed Okonkwo in the television adaptation of Chinua Achebe ‘s Things Fall Apart , a performance that helped establish him as one of Nollywood’s most respected actors. The veteran actor passed away in Enugu yesterday, on Wednesday, 25 November 2026, at the age of 79, following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer. Born in Zaria and originally from Ifite Nteje in Anambra State, Edochie began his career in broadcasting in 1967, eventually rising to become Deputy Managing Director of the Anambra Broadcasting Service. He went on to feature in hundreds of films, including Igodo , The Egg of Life and Lionheart . Pete Edochie and Genevieve Nnaji behind the scenes on the set of the 2018 film Lionheart, where they played father and daughter Chief Ernest Obiagu and Adaeze Obiagu. Survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including actors Linc and Yul Edochie , he leaves behind a remarkable body of work. As we remember his life and contribution to Nigerian cinema, here are five films that capture some of the performances that made Pete Edochie a household name. Things Fall Apart (1987) Before Nollywood’s home-video boom even began, Pete Edochie became a household name across Nigeria and internationally through his breakout role as Okonkwo in the Nigerian Television Authority (NTA) adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s classic novel Things Fall Apart. Directed by David Orere , the acclaimed television miniseries marked Edochie’s first professional acting role and saw him bring the proud, fierce, and deeply conflicted Umuofia warrior to life with remarkable nuance. His performance was so transformative that, for generations of viewers, Edochie and Okonkwo became inseparable. Rituals (1997) As Nollywood entered its golden home-video era in the late 1990s, Edochie starred in Andy Amenechi’s gripping thriller Rituals as Don Pedro, a calculating member of a secretive and ruthless society. Trading his traditional royal regalia for sharp corporate power plays, Edochie anchored a cautionary drama about unchecked political ambition, greed, and moral compro

item.content:encoded: Nollywood icon Pete Edochie, MON, who passed away at the age of 79 in Enugu. Did you grow up watching Pete Edochie in Nollywood films? Then you probably remember that voice. Deep, commanding and unmistakable, it often came with his signature red cap, traditional Igbo attire and a generous helping of proverbs. The actor was just as memorable away from the screen, where his sharp wit, outspoken nature and candid opinions made him a fascinating personality in interviews. He was never one to shy away from saying exactly what he thought, and that straightforwardness became another part of what audiences remembered about him. For generations of Nollywood viewers, Pete Edochie was the actor they could recognise before he had even finished his first sentence. He became one of Nigerian cinema’s most familiar faces, often playing kings, chiefs, fathers and respected elders. His breakthrough came in 1987 when he portrayed Okonkwo in the television adaptation of Chinua Achebe ‘s Things Fall Apart , a performance that helped establish him as one of Nollywood’s most respected actors. The veteran actor passed away in Enugu yesterday, on Wednesday, 25 November 2026, at the age of 79, following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer. Born in Zaria and originally from Ifite Nteje in Anambra State, Edochie began his career in broadcasting in 1967, eventually rising to become Deputy Managing Director of the Anambra Broadcasting Service. He went on to feature in hundreds of films, including Igodo , The Egg of Life and Lionheart . Pete Edochie and Genevieve Nnaji behind the scenes on the set of the 2018 film Lionheart, where they played father and daughter Chief Ernest Obiagu and Adaeze Obiagu. Survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including actors Linc and Yul Edochie , he leaves behind a remarkable body of work. As we remember his life and contribution to Nigerian cinema, here are five films that capture some of the performances that made Pete Edochie a household name. Things Fall Apart (1987) Before Nollywood’s home-video boom even began, Pete Edochie became a household name across Nigeria and internationally through his breakout role as Okonkwo in the Nigerian Television Authority (NTA) adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s classic novel Things Fall Apart. Directed by David Orere , the acclaimed television miniseries marked Edochie’s first professional acting role and saw him bring the proud, fierce, and deeply conflicted Umuofia warrior to life with remarkable nuance. His performance was so transformative that, for generations of viewers, Edochie and Okonkwo became inseparable. Rituals (1997) As Nollywood entered its golden home-video era in the late 1990s, Edochie starred in Andy Amenechi’s gripping thriller Rituals as Don Pedro, a calculating member of a secretive and ruthless society. Trading his traditional royal regalia for sharp corporate power plays, Edochie anchored a cautionary drama about unchecked political ambition, greed, and moral compromise. His cool, authoritative delivery alongside co-stars including Richard Mofe – Damijo , Bob – Manuel Udokwu , and Eucharia Anunobi made the film one of the defining Nollywood thrillers of the decade. Igodo: The Land of the Living Dead (1999) In this landmark supernatural adventure directed by Andy Amenechi and Don Pedro Obaseki, Edochie played one of the principal elders guiding a cursed community desperate for salvation. The story follows seven chosen warriors sent into a perilous evil forest to retrieve a mystical sword capable of breaking the land’s curse. Sharing the screen with Sam Dede, Norbert Young, and Charles Okafor, Edochie grounded the high-stakes fantasy with his signature gravitas and mastery of Igbo proverbs. Veteran Nollywood actor Chief Dr Pete Edochie and his wife, Barrister Mrs Josephine Edochie, at a church service. Egg of Life (2003) Directed by Andy Amenechi , Egg of Life stands out as one of early-2000s Nollywood’s most beloved fantasy epics, with Edochie cast as the Igwe whose kingdom is thrown into crisis when his young heir falls gravely ill.When the chief priestess—played by Clarion Chukwura —reveals that only a sacred egg hidden deep within a spirit-guarded forest can save the prince’s life, a group of maidens embarks on a perilous quest. Edochie’s dignified portrayal of a father and monarch balancing royal duty with quiet vulnerability gave the film its emotional core. Lionheart (2018) For a younger global audience, Edochie’s performance as Chief Ernest Obiagu in Genevieve Nnaji ’s directorial debut Lionheart remains one of his most endearing screen appearances. Playing the respected founder of Lionheart Transport Company who is forced to step back due to health challenges, Edochie brought warmth, humour, and quiet wisdom to a modern family drama co-starring Genevieve Nnaji, Nkem Owoh , and Onyeka Onwenu . Released worldwide on Netflix in 2019, the film showcased his effortless transition into contemporary cinema. item.title: Microsoft hotpatches hotpatch that could crash Windows Server 2025
item.description: Microsoft has released an out-of-band hotpatch to fix a bug in November's Windows Server 2025 security update that could crash some servers when an IPv6 route expires. The patch for the patch, KB5138318 , addresses crashes on systems with Router Advertisement (RA) enabled that receive time-bound IPv6 routes. When a route timer expires, affected servers can halt with error 0x139 (KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE). Issued on November 25, the corrective update takes effect without requiring a restart, according to Microsoft. KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE means the kernel has detected corruption of a critical data structure and stopped the system. Microsoft has identified route-timer expiry as the trigger but hasn't explained the underlying coding fault. Good to see the operating system being protected against the impact of the corruption. Less good for administrators wondering why their servers have suddenly misbehaved. Lansweeper puts Windows Server 2025 at 7 percent of the servers it monitors, compared with 32 percent for Server 2022 and 33 percent for Server 2019. Only systems with the affected hotpatch and networking configuration are implicated. Microsoft's Windows Server updates have not gone well over the last few months, with out-of-band updates issued in September, October, and November. An out-of-band update to deal with a problem introduced in a hotpatch (in this case, KB5131077 ) therefore carries with it a certain sense of inevitability. Hotpatches are a way of getting OS security updates on a Windows Server without requiring a restart and so are, in theory, a boon for administrators keen on maximizing uptime. According to Microsoft, in addition to faster installations and better protection, there is "lower workload impact with less need to restart your machine." Avoiding a planned restart is less of a selling point when the alternative is an unplanned crash. ®
item.dc:creator: Richard Speed
item.content:encoded: Microsoft has released an out-of-band hotpatch to fix a bug in November's Windows Server 2025 security update that could crash some servers when an IPv6 route expires. The patch for the patch, KB5138318 , addresses crashes on systems with Router Advertisement (RA) enabled that receive time-bound IPv6 routes. When a route timer expires, affected servers can halt with error 0x139 (KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE). Issued on November 25, the corrective update takes effect without requiring a restart, according to Microsoft. KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE means the kernel has detected corruption of a critical data structure and stopped the system. Microsoft has identified route-timer expiry as the trigger but hasn't explained the underlying coding fault. Good to see the operating system being protected against the impact of the corruption. Less good for administrators wondering why their servers have suddenly misbehaved. Lansweeper puts Windows Server 2025 at 7 percent of the servers it monitors, compared with 32 percent for Server 2022 and 33 percent for Server 2019. Only systems with the affected hotpatch and networking configuration are implicated. Microsoft's Windows Server updates have not gone well over the last few months, with out-of-band updates issued in September, October, and November. An out-of-band update to deal with a problem introduced in a hotpatch (in this case, KB5131077 ) therefore carries with it a certain sense of inevitability. Hotpatches are a way of getting OS security updates on a Windows Server without requiring a restart and so are, in theory, a boon for administrators keen on maximizing uptime. According to Microsoft, in addition to faster installations and better protection, there is "lower workload impact with less need to restart your machine." Avoiding a planned restart is less of a selling point when the alternative is an unplanned crash. ®

item.title: Dozens of court cases in England and Wales affected by undisclosed AI use in 2026
item.description: Exclusive: Investigation finds at least 25 cases affected by AI-generated witness statements, fictitious case law and nonexistent statutes Undisclosed AI use has affected more than two dozen court cases this year, prompting judges to complain about AI-generated witness statements, fictitious case law and nonexistent statutes, an investigation has revealed. Proceedings where judges have been forced to deal with lawyers, police officers and claimants misusing the technology in 2026 include a high court dispute between tax lawyers marred by what the judge called “unacceptable” use of “generative AI hallucinations” and references to nonexistent cases. item.title: Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming
item.description: Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO 2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it. A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note. Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don't digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO 2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO 2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO 2 . That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane. Read full article Comments

item.title: Zecathon 6.0: Zenith Bank Injects ₦190 Million into Africa’s Tech Ecosystem to Scale Homegrown Solutions
item.description: In a powerful demonstration of its commitment to Africa’s digital and economic future, Zenith Bank has concluded Zecathon 6.0, its flagship startup competition and innovation program. Executed by Beyond Limits Global as its implementation partner, the competition deployed a staggering ₦190 Million in non-equity capital across three strategic tracks, reinforcing its position as a critical launchpad for the continent’s tech ecosystem. ​A Holistic Investment in The Innovation Pipeline This year’s event drew thousands of applications across Africa and introduced a wider, more inclusive format. The competition successfully spanned the entire innovation pipeline—from brilliant secondary school students testing their first ideas to seasoned developers building advanced AI architectures, and growth-stage startups ready to scale their market footprints. ​In her welcome remarks at the 2026 Zenith Bank Tech Fair, Dame Dr. Adaora Umeoji , OON, Group Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of Zenith Bank Plc, said: “ The next generation of global AI champions can and should come from Africa. This is why the Zecathon sits at the heart of this Tech Fair. It is our search for Africa’s most promising innovators, across every sector, and our commitment is to support them with capital, mentorship and incubation.” Echoing this commitment, Lanre Oladimeji , General Manager at Zenith Bank & MD of Finopay , noted the strategic necessity of the platform. “The financial services sector thrives on continuous evolution. The solutions presented across these tracks—from inclusive voice-first banking to digital procurement platforms—are the exact kind of robust, user-centric technologies that will shape the next generation of our digital economy.” ​ “Zecathon 6.0 represents a deliberate investment in the depth and long-term potential of Africa’s innovation ecosystem. Beyond creating a platform for showcasing ideas, it is about strengthening the connections between talent, technology, entrepreneurship and industry, and creating pathways for innovation to translate into tangible economic and social value. Ultimately, the ambition is to build an ecosystem where innovation can thrive, businesses can grow and solutions can create lasting impact,” said Fikun Aluko , Innovation Expert and Co-lead of the Zecathon 6.0 Program. Expanding on the program’s design and execution, Daniel Iyiola , Program Manager at Beyond Limits Global, said: “Zecathon 6.0 was designed around a deliberate approach to engaging innovation at different stages of development. Executed by Beyond Limits Global as its implementation partner, the competition deployed a staggering ₦190 Million in non-equity capital across three strategic tracks, reinforcing its position as a critical launchpad for the continent’s tech ecosystem. ​A Holistic Investment in The Innovation Pipeline This year’s event drew thousands of applications across Africa and introduced a wider, more inclusive format. This is why the Zecathon sits at the heart of this Tech Fair. It is our search for Africa’s most promising innovators, across every sector, and our commitment is to support them with capital, mentorship and incubation.” Echoing this commitment, Lanre Oladimeji , General Manager at Zenith Bank & MD of Finopay , noted the strategic necessity of the platform. “The financial services sector thrives on continuous evolution. The solutions presented across these tracks—from inclusive voice-first banking to digital procurement platforms—are the exact kind of robust, user-centric technologies that will shape the next generation of our digital economy.” ​ “Zecathon 6.0 represents a deliberate investment in the depth and long-term potential of Africa’s innovation ecosystem. Beyond creating a platform for showcasing ideas, it is about strengthening the connections between talent, technology, entrepreneurship and industry, and creating pathways for innovation to translate into tangible economic and social value. Ultimately, the ambition is to build an ecosystem where innovation can thrive, businesses can grow and solutions can create lasting impact,” said Fikun Aluko , Innovation Expert and Co-lead of the Zecathon 6.0 Program. Expanding on the program’s design and execution, Daniel Iyiola , Program Manager at Beyond Limits Global, said: “Zecathon 6.0 was designed around a deliberate approach to engaging innovation at different stages of development. The Startup Pitch Competition challenged growth-stage businesses to demonstrate commercial traction, market relevance and the capacity to scale. The Innovation Hackathon placed emphasis on applied problem-solving, technical execution and the development of working solutions to real-world challenges, while the Future Innovators Challenge created an avenue for senior secondary school students to engage with technology, creativity and innovation from an early stage. Bringing these distinct pathways together allowed the program to recognise established innovation, test emerging solutions and nurture the next generation of talent.” ​Startup Pitch Competition: Accelerating Growth-Stage Ventures The Startup Pitch Competition saw fierce competition among 21 semi-finalists drawn from a pool of 1,609 African applicants. The ₦90 million prize pool for this track was led by Cutstruct Technology Limited, which secured ₦35 million for an innovative digital procurement platform seamlessly connecting developers, contractors, and financiers in the construction sector. ​The top five was completed by ventures demonstrating high-impact solutions across key economic sectors: Sproutly (₦20 million) for a financial infrastructure platform helping schools manage operations and fee payments; PharmaRun (₦15 million) for a technology-powered network ensuring last-mile medication access; AUI BRAND (₦10 million) for locally manufactured, deep-tech medical equipment aimed at reducing newborn mortality; and ProDevs (₦10 million) for an AI-powered HR platform streamlining global hiring. ​Innovation Hackathon: Engineering the Future of Finance Bringing an unprecedented level of technical rigor to the event, the Innovation Hackathon tasked developers with solving complex banking challenges. Twenty shortlisted teams out of 1,213 applicants participated in an intense three-day, in-person coding sprint. ​The ₦90 million hackathon prize pool was topped by Team Solo, winning ₦35 million for engineering a highly inclusive banking application featuring customizable voice and sign-language modes for diverse accessibility needs. 10x Brains secured ₦20 million for an instant fraud-prevention verification layer, and Rumour Hunters won ₦15 million for an AI-driven transaction diagnostic platform. Òmìnira (₦10 million) and Team Avera (₦10 million) were also rewarded for pioneering a voice-first accessibility tool with sonar selfies and building an autonomous AI incident laboratory, respectively. Future Innovators Challenge: Empowering the Next Generation Ensuring the pipeline of future talent remains robust, the Future Innovators Challenge tasked senior secondary school students with developing community-driven solutions. Following an intensive three-day design-thinking bootcamp and final showcase, three brilliant schools emerged victorious from a pool of 114 applications, sharing a ₦10 million prize pool. Caleb British International School , Lagos, emerged as the overall winner, claiming ₦5 million for ReLearn, a technology-enabled textbook recovery platform giving unused books a second life. Queen of the Rosary College, Onitsha, secured second place (₦3 million) for SabiCare, a gamified platform teaching life-saving first aid through story-based simulations. Regina Pacis International Secondary School, Onitsha, came third (₦2 million) for FireHearts, an IoT-powered safety system designed to detect dangerous gas leaks and prevent household fires. Beyond the Capital: Building Sustainable Enterprises To ensure these solutions transition from competition winners to sustainable, market-ready enterprises, the top teams from the Hackathon and Business Pitch tracks will undergo a rigorous two-week development program. This post-event accelerator is designed to complement their financial backing with executive leadership training, ecosystem networking, and technical refinement. For more updates, visit and follow @zenithbankplc and @the_beyondlimits on social media. item.title: Dressmaker review – delightful business sim is a cut above
item.description: PC; Cosy Lives/Free Lives Catering to the exacting whims of a small town preparing for some grand visitors presents absorbing, beautifully designed – and surprisingly thrilling – challenges The small town of Twillford is abuzz with intrigue and excitement. A local duke has died and ladies of a certain standing are determined to make an impression at the funeral. As a newly arrived dressmaker with the only clothing shop in the area, you’re about to get plenty of work. Thus begins this utterly delightful sim game, in which you talk to customers, gather their style preferences and tailor specific outfits just for them. It could be a suitably respectful funeral frock, with just a hint of style to catch the eye of the duke’s wealthy relatives, or perhaps a work outfit for a farmer who loves bright colours. Once you have your brief, you open your sketchbook and draft a pattern using fabric swatches and a pencil to colour in your design. Need something elegant? How about a strapless bodice. An outfit for the office? A pencil skirt is a good call. Continue reading...

item.title: From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices
item.description: Ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working. Since its beginnings in 1998, Ars has never had a single, central office—a setup that makes for a great commute to work, with little risk of getting stuck in traffic. As Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices. We've got all sorts of setups, tucked into basements, dens, spare bedrooms, apartment corners, and lofts. They run the gamut from minimalist "here's my laptop and monitor" setups to "I really like collecting things." Without any further ado, let's dig in: Jeremy Hsu Living in a New York apartment means being smart with available space. Credit: Jeremy Hsu/Ars Technica As an apartment dweller in New York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces. My current hodgepodge of equipment is probably on the minimal side compared to many members of the Ars team. Read full article Comments

item.title: UK government working 'around the clock' on Capita contingency plans
item.description: The UK government is working "around the clock" on contingency plans for Capita contracts after the outsourcer's CEO quit and its shares plunged, a Cabinet Office minister told MPs. Capita announced plans this week to raise around £190 million through a share issue in the first half of 2027 after warning of sharply lower profits and further costs linked to its Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) contract. The outsourcer "should be absolutely ashamed of its performance" on the £239 million contract , Sally Jameson, parliamentary secretary in the Cabinet Office, told MPs on Tuesday . "We have seen evidence that it has stepped up in recent months and begun to rectify the problem, but it is inexcusable that it let the situation get to this point," she said. Adolfo Hernandez stepped down as CEO with immediate effect on Monday, with finance chief Pablo Andres taking over. Shares fell around 70 percent following the announcement. In the House of Commons, Jameson was asked about the government's plans if Capita were unable to carry out the remainder of its contract given the outsourcer's performance on the CSPS. "On contingency planning, it is important that we stabilize the situation and that Capita can continue to deliver the pension scheme. However, the government is working across departments, as we do in relation to all strategic suppliers, to ensure that the relevant contingency plans are in place. People are working around the clock on that," she said. Jameson said contingency planning for the pension scheme was already underway before Monday's announcement, describing it as standard practice for major government suppliers. She told the Chamber that the Cabinet Office was "currently arranging to meet the new CEO in the coming days" following Hernandez's departure. The Register first exposed problems with Capita's CSPS portal last December. The site, serving 1.5 million current and former public servants, rejected login details even for newly created accounts, contained broken and circular links, and displayed dummy text. In January this year, the Cabinet Office was forced to promise "interim support measures" for the CSPS following Capita's botched takeover, including 150 additional government staff to clear the backlog in cases. Speaking in Parliament, Conservative MP Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair of the Public Accounts Committee, said there had been "some tragic and dreadful cases" since Capita took over administration last December. "I heard of one poor lady who was living on benefits because she could not get the bereavement payments she needed after her sister's death. I have heard of a member of parliamentary staff, not far from this Chamber, who is having to delay his retirement by a year because he cannot even get a statement from the scheme." The government has withheld nearly £10 million in contractual payments over Capita's performance. It is currently locked in negotiations over further penalties following the appointment of an auditor

Jameson said contingency planning for the pension scheme was already underway before Monday's announcement, describing it as standard practice for major government suppliers. She told the Chamber that the Cabinet Office was "currently arranging to meet the new CEO in the coming days" following Hernandez's departure. The Register first exposed problems with Capita's CSPS portal last December. The site, serving 1.5 million current and former public servants, rejected login details even for newly created accounts, contained broken and circular links, and displayed dummy text. In January this year, the Cabinet Office was forced to promise "interim support measures" for the CSPS following Capita's botched takeover, including 150 additional government staff to clear the backlog in cases. Speaking in Parliament, Conservative MP Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair of the Public Accounts Committee, said there had been "some tragic and dreadful cases" since Capita took over administration last December. "I heard of one poor lady who was living on benefits because she could not get the bereavement payments she needed after her sister's death. I have heard of a member of parliamentary staff, not far from this Chamber, who is having to delay his retirement by a year because he cannot even get a statement from the scheme." The government has withheld nearly £10 million in contractual payments over Capita's performance. It is currently locked in negotiations over further penalties following the appointment of an auditor, first revealed in July. At the time, Hernandez apologized for Capita's performance but refused to commit to further compensation . The National Audit Office and Public Accounts Committee have both launched probes into Capita's handling of the CSPS and its appointment as a contractor. In February, The Register revealed a legal challenge to the government's award of the separate Synergy shared services contract to Capita. The deal covers HR and finance services across four Whitehall departments and associated arm's-length bodies. Rival bidder Sopra Steria, which owns incumbent provider SSCL, alleges Capita's bid was abnormally low and its proposed staffing raised concerns about delivery. Capita and the Department for Work and Pensions, which led the procurement, deny the allegations and say the competition was fair and open. Capita values the contract at £370 million. The Public and Commercial Services Union is now calling on the government to scrap Capita's shared services contract with the DWP , citing the outsourcer's troubled handling of CSPS. ®

item.title: Hackers help themselves to 1Password's source code and customer data
item.description: 1Password is reassuring customers that their vaults remain secure after an attacker breached its systems and stole account information and private source code. The Canadian security biz disclosed this week that an attacker had compromised an employee's corporate GitHub account, made off with private source code, and deployed malicious code to its backend services to siphon off customer information. 1Password, which began investigating the intrusion on November 19, hasn't said how many customers were affected, but confirmed that the stolen data includes names and email addresses used to sign in to the service, account identifiers, timestamps showing when users created and last accessed their accounts, and various pieces of non-secret account metadata. The company insists the information that customers actually pay it to protect was beyond the intruder's reach. "At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password said. Arguably more troubling is the revelation that the intruder gained access to 1Password's continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) infrastructure, which houses credentials used to keep its products running. The company says it has rotated or revoked potentially exposed credentials and that neither its apps nor its browser extensions were affected. 1Password hasn't explained how access to an employee's GitHub account enabled the attacker to deploy malicious code to its backend services, nor has it detailed the extent of the attacker's access to its software build and distribution infrastructure. The company did not respond to The Register's questions. The miscreant also got their hands on tokens embedded in emails sent to some customers as part of account invitations, provisioning, and recovery processes. These tokens aren't enough to access an account on their own, according to 1Password, as users must also authenticate via single sign-on or enter a verification code sent to their registered email address. The company says it specifically notified the small number of users with affected provisioning or recovery processes underway. It found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed provisioning tokens. Still, the breach has prompted the password management biz to beef up those verification codes, replacing the six-digit numeric variety with ten-character alphanumeric codes to make brute-forcing them considerably more difficult. 1Password has booted the intruder out of its GitHub environment, revoked the stolen token, and rolled back the affected backend services to clean versions of the code. It's since shored up security around its development infrastructure and employees' devices, and brought in outside security specialists to review its handiwork. The incident recalls the first stage of LastPass's 2022 breach, when an attacker compromised its development environment and stole source code. The incident recalls the first stage of LastPass's 2022 breach, when an attacker compromised its development environment and stole source code. Information obtained in that intrusion helped enable a second attack that exposed customer vault backups, including encrypted passwords. The UK Information Commission's Office slapped LastPass with a £1.2 million ($1.6 million) fine last December over the incident, which compromised the personal information of up to 1.6 million UK users. Among the regulator's gripes was that LastPass had fallen short of the higher standard of security expected of a company entrusted with people's passwords. Customers aren't being asked to change their account passwords or Secret Keys, neither of which 1Password stores, although the company is warning users to be on the lookout for phishing attempts. A list of email addresses belonging to people known to use a particular password manager is a handy thing for a phisher to have, especially when said password manager has just given them a plausible pretext for getting in touch. ®

item.title: Space plants with hot sauce: What ISS astronauts will be eating on Thanksgiving (video)
item.description: null The astronauts on the International Space Station will celebrate Thanksgiving with some nontraditional fare. Well, NASA astronaut Anil Menon will, anyway. In a video the agency released on Monday (Nov. 23), Menon showed off some of the plants he and his crewmates are growing in orbit and told us what's in store for the greens. "We need plants to survive as we set up our moon base , and as we go to Mars , we're going to have to grow our own nutrition. So that's what we're doing this Thanksgiving," Menon said in the 2.5-minute video. Astronauts deliver a Thanksgiving message from the International Space Station in November 2026. From left: NASA's Luke Delaney and Anil Menon, the Canadian Space Agency's Joshua Kutryk and NASA's Jessica Watkins. (Image credit: NASA) "I plan on using this [plant] with a tortilla and some pasta and some hot sauce to make my Thanksgiving meal," added Menon, who was wearing a chef's toque for the occasion. "And I'm grateful for you and for my family at home." He passed the microphone to fellow NASA astronaut Luke Delaney, who didn't talk about food but expressed gratitude to his family, crewmates and support network on Earth . Next up was NASA's Jessica Watkins, who gave us a rundown of the broader Thanksgiving menu in space. "Some of what we'll be eating here — we've got some roasted turkey, some mac and cheese, some mashed potatoes, and some candied yams," Watkins said, showing off the small bags containing each of those comestibles. "So, we should be in good shape." The Canadian Space Agency 's (CSA) Joshua Kutryk spoke next. He said he'll eat rice and the space-grown plants, which he'll consume raw "because it reminds me of Earth, which I miss." All four of the astronauts then wished us a happy Thanksgiving and did some zero-g flips and rolls, sending the space plants on a bit of a ride. Delaney, Kutryk and Watkins are members of SpaceX's Crew-13 mission, which arrived at the International Space Station (ISS) on Oct. 1 . There's a fourth Crew-13 astronaut as well — Sergey Teteryatnikov, of the Russian space agency Roscosmos . That quartet shares the ISS with Menon and cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina, who arrived in July aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft. Astronauts tend to get major holidays off on the ISS, and to celebrate them together. Doing so reinforces the already-strong bonds the crewmates share and helps them deal with the pain of being away from friends and family, which can be especially acute on holidays like Thanksgiving and Christmas. Kutryk is likely feeling especially emotional these days. On Tuesday, the CSA announced that Kutryk's wife had given birth to the couple's third child, a daughter. "Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives," the couple said in a statement shared by the CSA. "We are very proud of our growing family and are looking forward to getting our little crew of five all reunited."

item.title: 45°C inlets just killed the chiller. Most people haven't noticed yet
item.description: SC25 in St. Louis looked like a plumbing convention cross booked the supercomputing hall. Pipes, pumps, manifolds, quick-disconnects, and a lot of people who clearly spend more time thinking about pressure drop than floating-point. I kept expecting to see a booth selling industrial fire hoses. Chicago is a much bigger building – McCormick has roughly four times the exhibit space St. Louis had – so the pre-show question was whether SC26 will still look like that or whether the hall is large enough to dilute the effect. If anything, cooling was even more dominant in Chicago. The heat problem didn't get smaller just because the building got bigger. We also saw a lot of new companies displaying their cooling wares at SC26. I follow this stuff closely and see two broad trends. First: consolidation with big industrial suppliers buying up the liquid cooling pioneers. Second: anyone with an angle is heading into the market. Both trends were visible on the floor in Chicago, and everyone had something to say about higher inlet temperatures, whether they have a real story or not. Game changing news The real news, though, is a number Nvidia dropped earlier this year: 45°C (113°F) liquid inlet temperature for their parts. That's not a small tweak. Most liquid-cooled systems have been living in the 30-35°C (86-95°F) world because that's what the chips would tolerate. Jump to 45°C (113°F) and a whole bunch of datacenters that currently need chillers suddenly don't. If AMD, Intel, and the Arm folks can match it – and we’d be shocked if they aren't already working on exactly that – then free cooling stops being a cool climate thing and becomes the default for a lot of places. Rooftop dry coolers can reject nearly any incoming fluid temperature and bring it below 45°C (113°F). There are few places in the world where ambient temperatures approach 113°F, and for the hours when outside temps spike, adiabatic assist is available. This is where water is trickled through a mesh surrounding the dry coolers, which drops the effective temperature another 10–20 percent. So, in our new cooling world, there are two closed loops: one taking heat from the server gear and then passing it to a second, different loop that takes the hot water to the roof, cools it, then brings it back again. What's missing here? It's the chillers. You won't need them anymore. These are essentially huge rooftop refrigerators that cool water even more after the dry cooling. They're expensive, need a lot of maintenance, gulp electricity and are thankfully unnecessary now for new datacenter builds. The power and water savings are not trivial. Legacy designs that rely on chillers and open evaporative towers commonly put 20 percent to 40 percent of total facility energy into cooling. A large share of that is the chiller plant itself – compressors, pumps, and cooling-tower fans. Move to dry coolers running at 45°C (113°F) inlet and that slice collapses. item.content:encoded: SC25 in St. Louis looked like a plumbing convention cross booked the supercomputing hall. Pipes, pumps, manifolds, quick-disconnects, and a lot of people who clearly spend more time thinking about pressure drop than floating-point. I kept expecting to see a booth selling industrial fire hoses. If anything, cooling was even more dominant in Chicago. The heat problem didn't get smaller just because the building got bigger. We also saw a lot of new companies displaying their cooling wares at SC26. I follow this stuff closely and see two broad trends. First: consolidation with big industrial suppliers buying up the liquid cooling pioneers. Second: anyone with an angle is heading into the market. Both trends were visible on the floor in Chicago, and everyone had something to say about higher inlet temperatures, whether they have a real story or not. Game changing news The real news, though, is a number Nvidia dropped earlier this year: 45°C (113°F) liquid inlet temperature for their parts. That's not a small tweak. Most liquid-cooled systems have been living in the 30-35°C (86-95°F) world because that's what the chips would tolerate. Jump to 45°C (113°F) and a whole bunch of datacenters that currently need chillers suddenly don't. If AMD, Intel, and the Arm folks can match it – and we’d be shocked if they aren't already working on exactly that – then free cooling stops being a cool climate thing and becomes the default for a lot of places. Rooftop dry coolers can reject nearly any incoming fluid temperature and bring it below 45°C (113°F). There are few places in the world where ambient temperatures approach 113°F, and for the hours when outside temps spike, adiabatic assist is available. This is where water is trickled through a mesh surrounding the dry coolers, which drops the effective temperature another 10–20 percent. So, in our new cooling world, there are two closed loops: one taking heat from the server gear and then passing it to a second, different loop that takes the hot water to the roof, cools it, then brings it back again. What's missing here? It's the chillers. You won't need them anymore. These are essentially huge rooftop refrigerators that cool water even more after the dry cooling. They're expensive, need a lot of maintenance, gulp electricity and are thankfully unnecessary now for new datacenter builds. The power and water savings are not trivial. Legacy designs that rely on chillers and open evaporative towers commonly put 20 percent to 40 percent of total facility energy into cooling. A large share of that is the chiller plant itself – compressors, pumps, and cooling-tower fans. Move to dry coolers running at 45°C (113°F) inlet and that slice collapses. Published estimates and vendor modeling for high-temperature liquid loops put the reduction in cooling energy in the 50 percent to 70 percent range versus a conventional chiller-plus-tower plant, which translates into a 10 percent to 20 percent drop in total datacenter power – depending on the starting PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) and climate. Water use falls even harder. Traditional evaporative towers can consume millions of gallons a year at a mid-size site. Dry coolers use essentially no outside water in normal operation; adiabatic assist only wets the mesh during the hottest hours, cutting annual water consumption by 80 percent to 95 percent in most climates. Those are the numbers that make the 45°C (113°F) inlet such a big deal. The same shift also changes the economics of the mechanical plant itself. A chiller plant is not just an operating cost; it is capital equipment that has to be sized, installed, maintained, and eventually replaced. Dry coolers are simpler, cheaper to install, and have far fewer moving parts. When the chips will accept 45°C (113°F) fluid, the business case for putting a mechanical refrigeration plant on the roof of a new build gets hard to defend in most climates. That is the part that has not yet fully registered outside the cooling specialists. Getting to 45°C isn't free Designing systems around these higher inlet temperatures still takes real engineering work – sizing the loops, choosing the dry coolers, and making sure the facility can run at the new set points without surprises. Existing buildings add another layer. Many were built with pipes, pumps, and heat exchangers sized air cooling or lower temperature liquid. Raising liquid inlet temperature means checking flow rates, pressure drops, and making sure the existing set-up delivers. At SC26 I had meetings with a couple of companies that do this work and buttonholed more in their booths. My top-of-mind questions were: Are the 45°C (113°F) inlet temps for real? Yes, they are, and are being used as a design basis to an extent – they need to leave headroom, of course. Any news on whether the other chipmakers are going to hit the Nvidia number on inlet temperature? Attendees were closed-lipped on this one. Nothing public from the other vendors (AMD/Intel/Arm). But on the cooling vendor side, they are happy to see the increase and will comply. My instincts are telling me that the other chipsters may have been caught flatfooted by Nvidia's 45°C stake in the ground, but those same instincts also tell me that handfuls of Peanut M&Ms healthy snacks. I’ll nose around more. There's real money at stake here from a TCO standpoint. One cooling vendor reports that their initial testing shows 3 percent to 4 percent cooling energy cost decrease for every additional 1°C inlet temperature increase. That's a significant number at scale. We're approaching a point where industry advances are answering many of the objections (the real ones, not the hysterical ones) raised by the anti-data center movement. Much lower energy use, water consumption down by 85 percent to 90 percent, higher efficiency and lower costs. Not a bad deal, right? ®

item.title: Chewing Stick or Toothbrush: Which is Better for Your Teeth?
item.description: Close-up of a woman brushing her teeth as part of her daily dental hygiene routine. Image by PNW Production for Pexels A toothbrush with fluoride toothpaste is the better choice for protecting your teeth against cavities, but chewing sticks are real cleaning tools too. Some studies have found that using a chewing stick alongside brushing can help remove more plaque and reduce gum inflammation. So if you grew up with a chewing stick, you do not need to feel embarrassed about it. Can a chewing stick clean your teeth as well as a toothbrush? In studies with adults , certain chewing sticks can clean your teeth about as well as a toothbrush for plaque and gum health, as long as you use them properly. Plaque is the soft, sticky layer of bacteria that builds up on your teeth, and it can lead to gum disease and cavities. Studies of miswak , a type of chewing stick made from the Salvadora persica tree, have found that it can remove plaque and reduce gum inflammation about as effectively as a toothbrush. Some studies also found that people who used miswak alongside brushing had less plaque and less gum inflammation than people who only brushed. Nigerian chewing sticks come from many plants, including dogonyaro (neem) and orogbo (bitter kola). Not every type has been studied, so we cannot assume they all produce the same results . Why do dentists recommend a toothbrush with fluoride toothpaste? Dentists recommend a toothbrush with fluoride toothpaste because it protects against cavities, and a chewing stick cannot promise that. Fluoride toothpaste is proven to reduce tooth decay compared with toothpaste without fluoride. The American Dental Association recommends brushing twice a day with it. The chewing stick studies discussed measured plaque and gum health, not cavities. Unlike fluoride toothpaste, a chewing stick doesn’t provide a reliable amount of fluoride to help protect your teeth against decay. A toothbrush typically reaches the inner surfaces of your teeth more effectively because the bristles are aligned with the handle. The best routine is to brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and use your chewing stick as an extra if you like it. Clean between your teeth once a day with floss or an interdental brush, which is a tiny brush made for the gaps between teeth. Neither a chewing stick nor a toothbrush fully cleans those spaces. How do you use a chewing stick without hurting your gums? If you’re to use a chewing stick, use it gently and keep it fresh. First, peel back about half an inch of bark and chew the tip until it frays soft like a brush. Then clean with short strokes moving away from the gum, because hard side-to-side scrubbing can irritate your gums. Replace the tip when it becomes worn or stiff, since a rough tip is harder on your gums, and keep your strokes light. First, peel back about half an inch of bark and chew the tip until it frays soft like a brush. Then clean with short strokes moving away from the gum, because hard side-to-side scrubbing can irritate your gums. Replace the tip when it becomes worn or stiff, since a rough tip is harder on your gums, and keep your strokes light. When you have a tooth problem, always t ell your dentist exactly what you use so they can give you advice that fits your routine. You could say, “I use a chewing stick most mornings, and I also brush with toothpaste. Can you check my teeth and gums and show me if there’s anything I should change?” If you notice bleeding gums, sensitivity near your gumline or gums that seem to be pulling back, book a dental check-up. These symptoms can have different causes, and your dentist can help identify what’s happening. Whichever one you use, you are allowed to mention it to your dentist. item.title: A vocal cohort of tech leaders celebrates Huang’s Nvidia return, but others are keeping quiet
item.description: Elon Musk and Sam Altman among those rejoicing but Google, Meta and Apple chiefs have declined to weigh in The phrase “return of the king” rippled across social media on Monday. A vocal subsection of the tech industry was celebrating the resurrection of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. item.title: UK Home Office waved through border system without a working fix for bad data
item.description: The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded the UK Home Office over a border watchlist system launched without an effective way to correct inaccurate personal information. The regulator said the failings risked people being wrongly detained for additional checks at the UK border, potentially causing distress and other harm. The platform in question, Helios, was slated to replace its predecessor, Warnings Index, in September 2024 and despite an initial delay due to concerns over data quality, went live the following month. Both Helios and Warnings Index are watch-listing systems, designed to allow law enforcement officials – mainly but not exclusively Border Force – to check people's data against official records at the UK border. Helios's federated operating model, whereby the data sources are not centrally managed, yielded quicker results than Warnings Index, but contained a critical flaw in that operational staff could not alter incorrect records. Platform operators, such as Border Force officers, could not amend the data that feeds into it, neither after the fact nor in real time. This was not the case with Warnings Index, which had a dedicated team responsible for correcting data entries in real time. Under Helios, staff were supposed to report inaccuracies to the organization responsible for the relevant source data, which would make the correction. One slight problem: there was no established reporting system at the time Helios was launched on October 2. The platform went live anyway, as officials deemed the data integrity and security risks presented by Warnings Index to be greater than those of Helios. Just nine days passed before the Home Office's data protection officer had to submit a breach report after Helios operational staff said they didn't know how to request data corrections. During the time, Helios operators sent 87 data rectification requests to the Warnings Index correction team, despite it having no capability to make the required changes to the data. The Home Office later said that many other requests likely weren't logged as the proper processes were not in place, and that staff should have logged the issue through a ServiceNow IT ticket, as any other departmental civil servant with any kind of IT issue would have. But the Home Office also said that including personal data in those helpdesk tickets would itself constitute a data breach. The ICO said in its reprimand document [PDF] that it is "unclear" how such a reporting arrangement could realistically work in practice, given that a report would require details from a subject's record that required rectification as well as the new, accurate information that should be used to replace it. The Home Office's proposed workaround was to get operational staff to verbally read out said personal data over a phone call with the IT helpdesk – a procedure it described as possible "but cumbersome." item.dc:creator: Connor Jones
item.content:encoded: The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded the UK Home Office over a border watchlist system launched without an effective way to correct inaccurate personal information. The regulator said the failings risked people being wrongly detained for additional checks at the UK border, potentially causing distress and other harm. The platform in question, Helios, was slated to replace its predecessor, Warnings Index, in September 2024 and despite an initial delay due to concerns over data quality, went live the following month. Both Helios and Warnings Index are watch-listing systems, designed to allow law enforcement officials – mainly but not exclusively Border Force – to check people's data against official records at the UK border. Helios's federated operating model, whereby the data sources are not centrally managed, yielded quicker results than Warnings Index, but contained a critical flaw in that operational staff could not alter incorrect records. Platform operators, such as Border Force officers, could not amend the data that feeds into it, neither after the fact nor in real time. This was not the case with Warnings Index, which had a dedicated team responsible for correcting data entries in real time. Under Helios, staff were supposed to report inaccuracies to the organization responsible for the relevant source data, which would make the correction. One slight problem: there was no established reporting system at the time Helios was launched on October 2. The platform went live anyway, as officials deemed the data integrity and security risks presented by Warnings Index to be greater than those of Helios. Just nine days passed before the Home Office's data protection officer had to submit a breach report after Helios operational staff said they didn't know how to request data corrections. During the time, Helios operators sent 87 data rectification requests to the Warnings Index correction team, despite it having no capability to make the required changes to the data. The Home Office later said that many other requests likely weren't logged as the proper processes were not in place, and that staff should have logged the issue through a ServiceNow IT ticket, as any other departmental civil servant with any kind of IT issue would have. But the Home Office also said that including personal data in those helpdesk tickets would itself constitute a data breach. The ICO said in its reprimand document [PDF] that it is "unclear" how such a reporting arrangement could realistically work in practice, given that a report would require details from a subject's record that required rectification as well as the new, accurate information that should be used to replace it. The Home Office's proposed workaround was to get operational staff to verbally read out said personal data over a phone call with the IT helpdesk – a procedure it described as possible "but cumbersome." It took the Home Office more than a year to implement a temporary data-rectification method, which involved a BX Data Query tile on the IT Now platform, allowing Helios operators to securely report data accuracy issues. The new method went live on October 25, 2025. By March 18, 2026, the Home Office said the new process had received more than 6,500 correction requests and around 5,000 records had been removed. The ICO said it "remains concerned" about the efficacy of this method, given that operators cannot include personal data in the tile report, but the regulator is satisfied the problem is at least in part fixed. The Home Office also said it was aware of an increase in customer complaints following Helios's launch, and around 800 cases in which people were delayed at the UK border pending additional checks. It was unable to attribute a specific number of these to Helios's technical issues, however. "The Home Office further stated that it was not aware of any data subjects suffering distress as a result of using its services at the UK border," the ICO's report stated. A Home Office spokesperson told us: " W e take data protection extremely seriously. That is why we have co-operated fully with the Information Commissioner's Office. "We immediately removed all outdated records to minimize delays to passenger journeys and strengthened mechanisms to speed up updates. "Our processes will continue to be kept under review, ensuring we meet data protection obligations while protecting border security." Joanne Stones, investigations manager at the ICO, said: "People must be able to trust that decisions about their immigration status at the UK border are made with accurate, up to date information." She added: "They also have the right to expect that when information is inaccurate, there is a swift and efficient way for it to be corrected. "We recognize that federated systems like Helios present unique challenges and welcome the steps the Home Office has taken since this issue was identified. However, the Home Office must ensure that its permanent solution provides a robust and effective way to identify and correct inaccurate information without delay." The ICO's public sector enforcement policy favors guidance, reprimands, and other interventions, reserving fines for the most egregious cases. Its rationale is to avoid diverting money from public services and effectively punishing those affected twice. Fines have included £350,000 for a 2021 MoD email that exposed details of Afghan evacuation applicants , and £750,000 for the PSNI's 2023 disclosure of workforce information , including surnames, initials, ranks, and roles. The PSNI penalty was reduced from £5.6 million under the public sector approach. ®

item.title: ‘Spiraling’ Final Trailer: Toni Tones Has Everything to Lose in Nigerian Thriller Series, Debuting on KAVA Today!
item.description: The four-part series, also starring Jim Iyke , Seun Ajayi and Folu Storms , is now streaming exclusively on KAVA . An illicit affair threatens to upend the life of a successful tech entrepreneur in the final trailer for Spiraling , the Nigerian psychological thriller from creator and director Wande Thomas , unveiled to coincide with the series’ streaming debut. Toni Tones ( King of Boys , The Smart Money Woman ) stars as Sade, a woman whose professional success and carefully curated personal life begin to unravel following a single lapse in judgment. Against the backdrop of a historic election, what starts as a private indiscretion escalates into a web of deception, betrayal and unprecedented consequences. Jim Iyke ( Bad Comments , Merry Men 2 ), Seun Ajayi ( Japa , The Smart Money Woman ) and Folu Storms ( Red Circle , Baby Farm ) round out the principal cast. A new series of character posters has also been released alongside the final trailer, spotlighting the key players in the psychological thriller. Exploring the intersection of ambition, desire and power, the series examines the lengths people will go to protect their reputations, and what happens when they can no longer control the narrative. Spiraling is created and directed by Thomas, who also produces alongside Isoken Ogiemwonyi under their respective production banners, Urbangidi Showtime and Studio Ogiso . The four-part thriller marks the latest addition to KAVA’s growing slate of straight to series African scripted entertainment. Watch the final trailer and see the newly released character posters below: More character posters here All four episodes of Spiraling are now streaming exclusively on KAVA. item.title: AI solved the hardest problem in maths – is there anything it can’t do?
item.description: Alzheimer’s disease, involving amyloid plaques in the brain, will be tough for AI to solve JUAN GAERTNER/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY The progress AI has made in mathematics this year is nothing short of extraordinary. In January, I was impressed to see relatively minor open problems tackled with the help of AI . Now, AI is being used to solve the hardest problems in maths . The obvious next question is, if AI can do this, is there anything it can’t do? That is the inference that the AI companies want us to make, but, in reality, the answer is much more nuanced. Read more Mathematicians are amazed by ‘holy grail’ proof of Riemann hypothesis We see this messaging in claims that AI can “solve X”, where X is any field of human endeavour you care to name. Biology is a big one. “Cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, mental illness – these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade,” said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei while promoting the company’s recent initial public offering . “I think one day maybe we can cure all disease with the help of AI,” said Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, last year , adding that this could be “within the next decade or so”. This phenomenon isn’t new: I call it “physicist brain”, after the propensity for physicists to wade into areas outside their expertise and declare simple solutions. More broadly, it is called Nobel disease , after the many Nobel prizewinners who have gone on to make, shall we say, less evidenced-backed claims. In general, there is a tendency to think that if an intelligent person is good at one thing, they are good at many other things that require intelligence. What is different now is that trillion-dollar companies and large swathes of the global economy now depend on this being true of artificial intelligence. Advertisement To be clear, I think we must now admit that AI is better at solving open mathematical problems than any human, and that this has happened faster than anyone ever expected. When I first saw the news in September that the Navier-Stokes problem had been solved by OpenAI , I felt stunned. We had entered a new world. With the announcement of the Riemann hypothesis proof this week, I felt sick and had to go and have a lie-down. These were intellectual Everests I have marvelled at since my teenage years, conquered by a machine far sooner than anyone expected. You may have read my recent piece forecasting the future in 2096 – an early draft had a line, later removed, about three Millennium Prize Problems being solved by AI in the 2030s. We’ve had two this year alone. But maths isn’t biology. Yes, we have seen advances like AlphaFold, Deepmind’s AI that can predict the structure of proteins , but this is biology at its most mathematical, a computational puzzle. True advances in biology and medicine require studying cells, animals and people, all of which can be frustratingly illogical and uncooperative.
